speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether the Ministry keeps track of the number of employees with remote working arrangements and the number of hours spent working remotely in the past year; (b) whether work-from-home (WFH) will become a permanent feature even as COVID-19 restrictions are relaxed; and (c) whether the Ministry will look into introducing new legislation to improve the welfare of WFH employees including barring employers from contacting employees about non-critical work matters outside of their contracted working hours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Manpower as companies are encouraged to operate in a hybrid operating model to boost business resilience (a) how will the Ministry support employers to help their employees transit towards this model; and (b) how will the Government encourage organisational dexterity in local companies so that work projects based overseas can be managed remotely from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: asked the Minister for Manpower whether, beyond the Tripartite Standards or Tripartite Guidelines, the Ministry intends to retain existing work-from-home legislation and make the right to work from home the new normal.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: COVID-19 has catalysed a transformation of workplace practices.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Businesses have adapted well and successfully implemented work-from-home arrangements.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: SMEs can also tap on Government grants, such as the Productivity Solution Grant, to adopt suitable cloud-based digital solutions that can enable productive remote work arrangements for their employees.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We expect work-from-home arrangements to become a more mainstream option.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Our approach for workplace flexibility should be inclusive and not just about working from home.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The 2019 Citizens' Panel on Work-Life Harmony highlighted the diverse needs of various sectors and jobs, such as the needs of frontline workers differing significantly from that of office workers.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For example, work-from-home is not practical for work that most frontline workers perform.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It is therefore critical that a holistic approach be taken to enable more workers' access to appropriate workplace flexibilities, be it flexi-load, flexi-time or flexi-place.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: To this end, the tripartite partners have been reaching out to employers and unions to promote the Tripartite Standard on Flexible Work Arrangements.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We had also formed the Alliance for Action (AfA) on Work-Life Harmony last year, involving community stakeholders such as employers, employees and HR professionals.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The AfA created three Communities of Practice for the food services, manufacturing and finance sectors respectively, to exchange best practices and develop implementation resources that were suited to companies’ sectoral needs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For example, Communities of Practice panellists shared how staggered hours could still be offered to onsite production staff who required them to flexibly manage their personal responsibilities, such as childcare.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The HR profession through the Institute of Human Resource Professionals also came together to develop the Playbook on Hybrid Workplaces.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We are continuing this ground-up effort by growing a community of Work-Life Ambassadors to champion and support these efforts at their workplaces.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Even as work-from-home arrangements stabilise, we are mindful of the risks from blurred work-life boundaries.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-being was introduced in 2020 and one of the key recommendations was for employers to set reasonable expectations of after-hours work communications, such as not requiring employees to respond to non-urgent work-related messages and emails after certain hours.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The AfA on Work-Life Harmony also developed an after-hours communications policy template to make it easier for companies to establish and communicate progressive after-hours communications practices.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government will continue to work with tripartite partners to expand the provision of flexible work arrangements in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, I am not asking for 100% compulsory work-from-home, but to legislate the right to work from home and also to give employers the right to reject for work-related reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, for example, if there is a face-to-face meeting that day, then the employee would not be allowed to work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, I do agree with the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should not jump into legislating things, but the fact is that we have been debating this right to work from home for quite a number of years in the House now, even in the pre-COVID-19 days.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: COVID-19 has shown that work-from-home is possible, so I am just wondering what is stopping MOM from legislating this right to work from home.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The number of workers with access to flexible work arrangements has increased steadily over the years.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: During the pandemic crisis, work-from-home as a form of flexible work arrangement has also become more common.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Member asked why do we not legislate the right to request for work-from-home.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: While the economy is showing signs of recovery and more employers and employees are more comfortable and used to the arrangement of work-from-home, there remain uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: As we look at other countries that have introduced legislation to allow employees to request to work from home, it is uncertain as in the outcomes are rather mixed on whether legislation makes a substantial improvement in the work-life and the flexibility that employees have.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: After all, like the hon Member said, employers will also have the right to reject the request for work-from-home.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I think we have to take a practical approach towards this.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I fully agree with the hon Member Louis Ng that legislation may not be the best solution.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In fact, what I think we should focus is on enabling employers and employees with resources and with guides to help them implement work-from-home and flexible work arrangements in a practical and sustained manner.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I note that the Ministry does not want to impose rigidity in workplace arrangements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can I ask what are the plans for the Ministry to enhance or update existing legislation like the Employment Act, Occupational Safety and Health Act, Work Injury Compensation Act and so on, to cover work-from-home situations and essentially, to cover the home as a workplace?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Employment Act covers basic terms of employment such as timely payment of salary and leave benefits.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The protections offered under the Employment Act are not location specific.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, whether an individual is working from home or working in the office or working in the factory, the Employment Act covers them.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There is a checklist that helps employers as well as employees identify hazards when they are working from home.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The key is about proving that the injury is incurred while a person is doing work and not performing non-work-related duties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The first is the tripartite advisory has been launched for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How many companies have actually adopted some of the advice that we have put out on work-life harmony?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My second supplementary question relates to a commentary written by a Financial Times writer that was republished on CNA just this morning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It mentioned the disconnect between how bosses find workers to be less productive when telecommuting and workers themselves feeling that they are busier than ever.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The writer argued that telecommuting makes workers busier simply because of the increased number of virtual meetings and having more internal coordination emails, work-related communications, but such additional work does not always translate to effective work outcomes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am of the view that we would need to come to a new social compact when it comes to such telecommuting work arrangements and reset expectations on what working hours are and what is productivity for those who work from home or those who adopt hybrid work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, can the Ministry study this issue in detail and provide recommendations on how workplaces can come to a consensus on such a new social compact and provide both employers and employees tools to manage the unique challenges posed by such telecommuting work arrangements?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC would be most happy to work with the Ministry on this.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I believe the hon Member Melvin Yong was referring to the Tripartite Standard on Flexible Work Arrangements and Tripartite Standard on Work-life Harmony.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Actually, the progress has been steadily increasing and we are quite glad for that.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Certainly, there is room for us to encourage more companies to come on board.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For bigger companies, probably, the confidence is a lot higher because they have the capacity and the expertise to implement flexible work arrangements and work-from-home arrangements more satisfactorily.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For small companies or SMEs, for example, there might be more help required.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And that is where the resources that have been put out by the tripartite partners, the Alliance for Action on Work-life Harmony, will come in useful.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will encourage companies to take a look at them.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I think we should give it some time for companies to take a look and also get our employees and unions to work with the employers to adopt this Standard.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The point about making further studies on how we should define productivity and how we need to safeguard employees from the ability to disconnect from work when they are working from home and not suffering burn-out, I think we have debated this last year.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It is important that we take practical approach towards this.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are people who may find that work-from-home suits them very well but we also know of individuals who prefer not to work from home, maybe because the home environment is not as conducive, perhaps they feel that their own productivity is not as high when they are working from home rather than in an office environment which is specially prepared for them to be able to work, interact and take part in team work and team meetings with their fellow workers.
